passages.title: The warning becomes the prophet's own lament
passages.summary: The LORD’s word comes to Micah of Moresheth about Samaria and Jerusalem. The LORD comes down, and the mountains melt under him. Samaria will become a heap of rubble. Its idols will be smashed. Micah says he will wail and go barefoot and naked. The wound has reached the gate of Jerusalem. He names town after town in Judah’s lowlands. Each one will share in the disaster and the exile.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected places named in the chapter. No army or promised return route is reconstructed.

lds.text: Why does Micah mourn while announcing judgment?

contextNote.title: The warning becomes the prophet's own lament
contextNote.text: Micah does not stand apart from his message. Verse 8 shows him mourning in public, stripped like a captive. The towns of verses 10–15 are his home region. Moresheth, his own village, is among them (verses 1 and 14). They lie on an invader’s road to Jerusalem. He announces judgment on his neighbors and grieves for them. Verse 9 says the wound has reached his people’s gate.

passages.title: Power turns private plans into public dispossession
passages.summary: Micah speaks against those who plan evil on their beds. At dawn they carry it out, since it is in their power. They covet fields and houses and seize them. They rob a man of his home and his inheritance. So God is planning disaster against them. They tell Micah not to preach such things. They drive women from their homes and take the children’s blessing. Yet God will gather the remnant like sheep.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter describes households and gathering without specifying mapped locations.

lds.text: Who loses shelter when powerful people seize inherited fields?

contextNote.title: Power turns private plans into public dispossession
contextNote.text: Verse 1 shows the order of events. The powerful plan at night and act at first light. They do it because they can. Verse 2 names what they take: fields, houses, and a family’s inheritance. Land in Israel was a family’s place among the people (Leviticus 25:23). Verse 9 shows women and children put out of their homes. They “devise” evil in verse 1, and God “devises” disaster in verse 3.

passages.title: Paid assurances hide the violence of rulers
passages.summary: Micah addresses the rulers of Israel, who should know justice. They hate good and treat the people like meat for the pot. Prophets promise peace to those who feed them. They declare war on those who give them nothing. Micah says he is filled with the LORD’s Spirit to declare Israel’s sin. Leaders judge for bribes, priests teach for pay, and prophets speak for money. They say the LORD is among them. So Zion will be plowed like a field.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected places named in the chapter. No army or promised return route is reconstructed.

lds.text: How does payment change the messages people receive?

contextNote.title: Paid assurances hide the violence of rulers
contextNote.text: Verse 11 names three offices with one motive. Judges, priests, and prophets all work for money. Verse 5 says a prophet’s message depends on who feeds him. They still claim that the LORD is among them. They treat his presence as a guarantee. Verse 12 answers that Zion will be plowed. A century later that verse was quoted to save Jeremiah’s life (Jeremiah 26:18).

passages.title: Peace means safety for those driven away
passages.summary: In later days the mountain of the LORD’s house will be raised above the hills. Nations will come to learn his ways. He will judge between peoples and settle their disputes. They will beat swords into plows and learn war no more. Everyone will sit under his own vine and fig tree, unafraid. God will gather the lame and those who were driven away. He will rule them on Mount Zion. For now Zion must go to Babylon, and there she will be rescued.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected places named in the chapter. No army or promised return route is reconstructed.

lds.text: In 3 Nephi 20:18–19 Jesus repeats the sheaves and iron horn. Who receives a place in the promised gathering?

contextNote.title: Peace means safety for those driven away
contextNote.text: Verses 1–3 match Isaiah 2:2–4 almost word for word. Micah adds verse 4. Peace is pictured at the size of one household. Each person has a vine and a fig tree and no fear. In 2:2 the powerful were seizing fields. Here no one takes them. Verses 6–7 say who is gathered: the lame and the outcast.

passages.title: A threatened ruler gives way to a shepherd
passages.summary: Jerusalem is under siege, and its ruler is struck on the cheek. A new ruler will come from Bethlehem, a small town in Judah. His origins are from ancient times. He will stand and shepherd his flock in the LORD’s strength. His people will live securely. He will be their peace when Assyria invades. The remnant of Jacob will be like dew among the nations. God will remove their horses, forts, and idols.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected places named in the chapter. No army or promised return route is reconstructed.

lds.text: The lesson’s children’s section connects Bethlehem with Jesus through Matthew’s account of his birth. How does feeding a flock change the image of a threatened ruler?

contextNote.title: A threatened ruler gives way to a shepherd
contextNote.text: Verse 1 shows a ruler humiliated in a besieged capital. Verse 2 looks away to Bethlehem, David’s village (1 Samuel 16:1). The new ruler comes from a small place. Verse 4 says he will “shepherd,” which means to feed and guard. His greatness rests on the LORD’s strength. The people’s gain is stated simply: they will live. Matthew 2:6 quotes verse 2 about the birth of Jesus.

passages.title: A dispute asks for conduct rather than greater payment
passages.summary: The LORD brings a case against his people, with the mountains as witnesses. He asks what he has done to weary them. He brought them from Egypt and sent Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. A worshiper asks what he should bring to the LORD. He offers calves, thousands of rams, and even his firstborn. The answer is that God has already shown what is good. Do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with God. The city, however, is full of false weights and violence.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected places named in the chapter. No army or promised return route is reconstructed.

lds.text: The lesson asks readers to consider the conduct Micah says God requires. How do false weights contradict the conduct God requires?

contextNote.title: A dispute asks for conduct rather than greater payment
contextNote.text: God speaks first as the one wronged and asks what he did (verse 3). The worshiper answers with rising offers in verses 6–7. He goes from calves to rivers of oil to his own child. Verse 8 says the answer was never a larger payment. God “has shown you” what is good. It names three things: just acts, loved mercy, and a humble walk. Verses 10–12 then point to false scales in the city’s markets.

passages.title: The appeal for mercy follows failed public trust
passages.summary: Micah grieves like someone who finds no fruit after the harvest. The faithful have vanished, and officials take bribes. No one can trust a neighbor or even a family member. Yet Micah will watch and wait for the LORD. He admits his sin and expects God to plead his case. He asks God to shepherd his people. He asks who is a God like this, who pardons guilt. God will hurl all their sins into the depths of the sea.
passages.uncertainty: Markers locate selected places named in the chapter. No army or promised return route is reconstructed.

lds.text: The lesson’s introduction emphasizes God’s delight in mercy through Micah’s final praise. Why does the ending join admitted wrongdoing with hope for forgiveness?

contextNote.title: The appeal for mercy follows failed public trust
contextNote.text: Verses 2–6 describe a society where no one can be trusted. That includes rulers, friends, and one’s own household. Hope cannot rest on the people around him. Verse 7 turns with “But as for me.” Verse 9 admits his own sin and accepts its weight. Verse 18 then praises a God who delights in loving kindness. Admitted wrong and hope of pardon stand together at the end.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Strong evidence supports this route. The line shows a general path. Its branches and exact roadbeds changed over time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The main connection is well supported. The line shows a broad route, not one fixed or fully built road.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The hill route is well supported. The exact track could divide or shift between nearby ridges and towns.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The valley route is well supported. The line combines several possible tracks. It does not mark specific river crossings.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional route is well supported. Local branches between valleys and fortified towns are simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact roadbed at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Lachish–Jerusalem approaches
ancientRoads.summary: Routes through the Shephelah valleys connected Lachish with Jerusalem. They also joined nearby walled towns with the Judean hills.
ancientRoads.detail: Second Kings 18:17 sends an Assyrian army from Lachish up to Jerusalem. The text does not name the road. This line shows one common approach.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is probable. The exact track is unknown, so the line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection is well supported. The displayed bends are approximate and do not identify one preserved Iron Age roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: This broad route is well known. It was not one fully built road. Its path and local branches remain uncertain.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is well supported. The evidence does not show one fixed Iron Age track. The line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Aleppo–Euphrates approach
ancientRoads.summary: This road linked Aleppo with the Euphrates crossing near Til Barsip. Assyria’s state road began there.
ancientRoads.detail: Assyrian records and studies of ancient land support this route. It went through the Sajur and Manbij area. It then crossed the Jabbul plain toward Aleppo.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection and principal approach are well supported. The displayed bends simplify several local valleys and possible parallel tracks.

ancientRoads.title: Assyrian King’s Road to Nineveh
ancientRoads.summary: The Neo-Assyrian state road connected western lands with the Assyrian heartland. It ended at the capital city of Nineveh.
ancientRoads.detail: The route crossed the Euphrates at Til Barsip. It crossed the Balih south of Harran. It also crossed Habur streams between Guzana and Nasibina. It then reached the Tigris at Nineveh. Royal messengers changed mules at road stations.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The named crossings and stations are well supported. The line between them is a broad regional path, not a surveyed roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Assyrian Tigris route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route followed the Tigris. It linked Nineveh, Kalhu, and Assur in the Assyrian heartland.
ancientRoads.detail: Kalhu held a central position between Assur and Nineveh. It supported long trips by land and river. Kalhu later became an Assyrian royal capital.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The cities and their connection are well supported. The line shows a broad route. It does not separate land travel from river travel at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Arbela–Babylonia route
ancientRoads.summary: An eastern branch connected Kalhu with Arbela. It followed the western edge of the Zagros Mountains. Other routes continued south into Babylonia.
ancientRoads.detail: Kalhu controlled an eastward route through Arbela. The route followed the western edge of the Zagros toward Babylonia. It avoided a direct crossing of the central desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is supported, but the precise southern alignment and stations are uncertain. The line is dashed.

regions.name: Kingdom of Israel · approximate
regions.summary: Ten tribes followed Jeroboam and formed a northern kingdom. Samaria became its capital under Omri.
regions.detail: Kings and Chronicles follow its kings beside Judah’s. Assyria takes Samaria and deports its people in 2 Kings 17.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Its borders with Aram, Moab, and Judah moved often.

regions.name: Kingdom of Judah · approximate
regions.summary: Judah was the southern kingdom. David’s family ruled it from Jerusalem for about four centuries.
regions.detail: Judah keeps David’s line when the north breaks away. Its kings fight Israel, pay it, and join it by turns.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. It is not a border for one year.

regions.name: Aram of Damascus · approximate
regions.summary: Aram was a kingdom centered on Damascus. Assyria ended it in 732 BCE.
regions.detail: Ben Hadad and Hazael fight Israel for Gilead. Naaman, healed in 2 Kings 5, commands Aram’s army.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Aram and Israel traded control of Gilead and Bashan.

regions.name: Phoenician cities · approximate
regions.summary: Tyre, Sidon, and other coast cities each had their own king. They lived by ships and trade.
regions.detail: Ahab marries Jezebel, daughter of the king of the Sidonians (1 Kings 16:31). Elijah stays with a widow at Zarephath near Sidon.
regions.uncertainty: The shape joins separate cities along one coast. They were never one kingdom.

regions.name: Philistine cities · approximate
regions.summary: Five Philistine cities held the southern coast: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, and Gath.
regions.detail: Philistine towns sit on Judah’s western border. Israel besieges Gibbethon, a Philistine town, twice in 1 Kings 15–16.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Each city had its own ruler.

regions.name: Ammon · approximate
regions.summary: Ammon was a kingdom east of the Jordan. Its chief city was Rabbah, now Amman.
regions.detail: Ammon joins Moab against Jehoshaphat in 2 Chronicles 20. Amos 1 accuses Ammon of cruelty in Gilead.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the land around Rabbah.

regions.name: Moab · approximate
regions.summary: Moab was a kingdom on the high land east of the Dead Sea. Dibon was its capital.
regions.detail: Mesha king of Moab rebels after Ahab dies (2 Kings 3). A stone that Mesha set up tells his side.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Numbers 21:26 says Moab once lost land north of the Arnon.

regions.name: Edom · approximate
regions.summary: Edom was a kingdom south of the Dead Sea. The Bible calls its people the children of Esau.
regions.detail: Edom revolts against Judah in the days of Jehoram (2 Kings 8:20–22). Amos 1 accuses Edom of chasing his brother with the sword.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Edom’s people later moved west into southern Judah.

regions.name: Egypt · approximate
regions.summary: Egypt’s kings ruled the Nile valley and delta.
regions.detail: Shishak king of Egypt takes the temple treasures from Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:25–26). Hosea warns Israel against calling on Egypt.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Egypt’s ruling families and power changed across these centuries.

regions.name: Assyria · home region
regions.summary: Assyria’s home lay on the upper Tigris around Assur, Kalhu, and Nineveh. From 745 BCE its kings pushed hard to the west.
regions.detail: Menahem of Israel and Ahaz of Judah pay Assyria’s kings. Assyria takes Damascus, then Samaria, in 2 Kings 16–17.
regions.uncertainty: The shape shows only the home region. Assyria’s reach to the west grew and shrank.

guides.title: Micah: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Power turns private plans into public dispossession
steps.text: Verse 1 shows the order of events. The powerful plan at night and act at first light. They do it because they can. Verse 2 names what they take: fields, houses, and a family’s inheritance. Land in Israel was a family’s place among the people (Leviticus 25:23). Verse 9 shows women and children put out of their homes. They “devise” evil in verse 1, and God “devises” disaster in verse 3.

steps.title: Peace means safety for those driven away
steps.text: Verses 1–3 match Isaiah 2:2–4 almost word for word. Micah adds verse 4. Peace is pictured at the size of one household. Each person has a vine and a fig tree and no fear. In 2:2 the powerful were seizing fields. Here no one takes them. Verses 6–7 say who is gathered: the lame and the outcast.

steps.title: A dispute asks for conduct rather than greater payment
steps.text: God speaks first as the one wronged and asks what he did (verse 3). The worshiper answers with rising offers in verses 6–7. He goes from calves to rivers of oil to his own child. Verse 8 says the answer was never a larger payment. God “has shown you” what is good. It names three things: just acts, loved mercy, and a humble walk. Verses 10–12 then point to false scales in the city’s markets.

chapterMaps.note: Markers locate selected places named in the chapter. No army or promised return route is reconstructed.
chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD’s word comes to Micah of Moresheth about Samaria and Jerusalem. The LORD comes down, and the mountains melt under him. Samaria will become a heap of rubble. Its idols will be smashed. Micah says he will wail and go barefoot and naked. The wound has reached the gate of Jerusalem. He names town after town in Judah’s lowlands. Each one will share in the disaster and the exile.
chapterMaps.limits: Markers locate selected places named in the chapter. No army or promised return route is reconstructed.

chapterMaps.note: The chapter describes households and gathering without specifying mapped locations.
chapterMaps.narrative: Micah speaks against those who plan evil on their beds. At dawn they carry it out, since it is in their power. They covet fields and houses and seize them. They rob a man of his home and his inheritance. So God is planning disaster against them. They tell Micah not to preach such things. They drive women from their homes and take the children’s blessing. Yet God will gather the remnant like sheep.
chapterMaps.limits: The chapter describes households and gathering without specifying mapped locations.

chapterMaps.note: Markers locate selected places named in the chapter. No army or promised return route is reconstructed.
chapterMaps.narrative: Micah addresses the rulers of Israel, who should know justice. They hate good and treat the people like meat for the pot. Prophets promise peace to those who feed them. They declare war on those who give them nothing. Micah says he is filled with the LORD’s Spirit to declare Israel’s sin. Leaders judge for bribes, priests teach for pay, and prophets speak for money. They say the LORD is among them. So Zion will be plowed like a field.

chapterMaps.note: Markers locate selected places named in the chapter. No army or promised return route is reconstructed.
chapterMaps.narrative: In later days the mountain of the LORD’s house will be raised above the hills. Nations will come to learn his ways. He will judge between peoples and settle their disputes. They will beat swords into plows and learn war no more. Everyone will sit under his own vine and fig tree, unafraid. God will gather the lame and those who were driven away. He will rule them on Mount Zion. For now Zion must go to Babylon, and there she will be rescued.

chapterMaps.note: Markers locate selected places named in the chapter. No army or promised return route is reconstructed.
chapterMaps.narrative: Jerusalem is under siege, and its ruler is struck on the cheek. A new ruler will come from Bethlehem, a small town in Judah. His origins are from ancient times. He will stand and shepherd his flock in the LORD’s strength. His people will live securely. He will be their peace when Assyria invades. The remnant of Jacob will be like dew among the nations. God will remove their horses, forts, and idols.
chapterMaps.limits: Markers locate selected places named in the chapter. No army or promised return route is reconstructed.

chapterMaps.note: Markers locate selected places named in the chapter. No army or promised return route is reconstructed.
chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD brings a case against his people, with the mountains as witnesses. He asks what he has done to weary them. He brought them from Egypt and sent Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. A worshiper asks what he should bring to the LORD. He offers calves, thousands of rams, and even his firstborn. The answer is that God has already shown what is good. Do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with God. The city, however, is full of false weights and violence.

chapterMaps.note: Markers locate selected places named in the chapter. No army or promised return route is reconstructed.
chapterMaps.narrative: Micah grieves like someone who finds no fruit after the harvest. The faithful have vanished, and officials take bribes. No one can trust a neighbor or even a family member. Yet Micah will watch and wait for the LORD. He admits his sin and expects God to plead his case. He asks God to shepherd his people. He asks who is a God like this, who pardons guilt. God will hurl all their sins into the depths of the sea.
